edge.title: The strip that looks right
edge.setup: You need a course of antibiotics, or a regular medicine for someone at home. An online listing or a small shop offers it noticeably cheaper than the chemist you normally use. The strip looks right, the box looks right, and the seller is cheerful about it. You have no way to read what is inside.
edge.tell: The price is below what every other chemist charges, or the seller cannot give you a bill showing the batch number.
move: Buy prescription medicines only from a licensed chemist, and ask for a printed bill that carries the batch number and expiry date.
Check that the batch number and expiry on the bill match what is printed on the strip and the outer box. A mismatch, smudged print or a re-stuck label means you stop there.
If a price is far below the going rate, treat it as the finding, not as a bargain. Compare it against a second licensed chemist before you buy.
If a medicine seems wrong or does nothing, keep the packaging and the bill and report it to the state drugs control department; do not throw the evidence away.
edge.why: You cannot verify a medicine yourself, so you rely on signals that are cheap to fake: the packaging, the brand name, a confident seller. The only part a counterfeiter cannot fake cheaply is a paper trail that runs back to a licensed supplier, and a price that makes sense. The mechanism is that the buyer knows least at the moment of purchase, and the seller knows exactly what is in the box. So you demand the one thing that moves information to your side: a bill with a batch number.
edge.variants: Same shape: counterfeit supplements and protein powder, refilled branded cosmetics, 'original' spare parts for a car or phone, re-sealed bottled water or cooking oil, a cheap 'sealed' phone with no invoice.
edge.anchor: The Times of India reports the ED raided premises in Bengaluru in a fake medicine racket case, froze ₹9 lakh in bank accounts, and found a farmhouse used to repackage antibiotics.

lens.name: Asymmetric information
lens.one_line: When one side knows much more than the other, the market degrades toward the worse goods.
lens.detail: If buyers can't tell good used cars from bad, they offer an average price. Owners of genuinely good cars refuse to sell at that price and leave the market, so the average quality drops, so the price drops further. Quality collapses — not from dishonesty, but from unverifiability. Every real fix is a verification mechanism: warranties, certification, inspection, reputation.
elsewhere: Freelance marketplaces race to the bottom without reviews.
Insurance pools get sicker when only the sick buy in.
A degree works partly as a costly signal of something an employer can't directly see.
lens.test: What can the other side see that I can't — and what would make it visible?
lens.today: The ED raid over antibiotics repackaged at a Bengaluru farmhouse is the whole model in one case: the seller knew what was in the box, and the buyer could only see a label. The same gap sits behind the Fevikwik gold-chain robbery story, where the shop could not tell the visitor from a customer. Where you cannot see inside, pay attention to what you can check, which is the bill, the batch and the price.

moved.so_what: Treat 13 November as the inauguration, not the day you can ride it; passenger service dates are normally announced separately. Expect heavier traffic around the event venue that day and plan any cross-town trip with an hour in hand.

moved.what: The Economic Times reports the INDIA bloc will hold an anti-SIR protest in Bengaluru on 5 November, and a Times of India piece has an MLA challenging claims of wrongful voter deletions.
moved.so_what: Check today that your name is on the electoral roll for your current address; it takes two minutes on the Election Commission's voter portal and the correction window is far easier to use now than at the polling booth. On 5 November, allow extra time for a protest-day diversion.

moved.what: The Times of India reports the Chief Minister has asked KMF to reconsider its curd price hike under pressure.
moved.so_what: The hike is not withdrawn yet, only under review. Do not stock up; buy as usual and look at the printed price on the next packet before assuming either way.

moved.what: The New Indian Express reports Karnataka Minister Krishna Byre Gowda saying the TDR system for road widening will be made digital.
moved.so_what: If your plot or building is on a widening alignment, ask for the TDR entry in writing and in the digital record once it goes live, and keep your own copy. A record that exists only on someone else's system is the weakest kind to hold.

carry_over.prompt: Part of your land is needed for a road, and you are offered a certificate or extra built-up area instead of cash: what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: You hand over the asset today; the paper's price gets set by someone else, later.
